title: Ὕαινα καὶ ἀλώπηξ
part: The Hyena and the Fox (Chambry 341 · Perry 242)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 341 (= Perry 242). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Τὰς ὑαίνας φασί, παρ’ ἐνιαυτὸν ἀλλασσομένης αὐτῶν τῆς φύσεως, ποτὲ μὲν ἄρσενας, ποτὲ δὲ θηλείας γίνεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Tas hyainas phasi, par’ eniauton allassomenēs autōn tēs physeōs, pote men arsenas, pote de thēleias ginesthai.
sentences.l: They say that hyenas, their nature changing in alternate years, become now males, now females.
sentences.n: The same opening as fable 340, with the construction recast: there the changing of nature was one of two coordinate infinitives (ἀλλάττειν … γίνεσθαι), here it is a genitive absolute (ἀλλασσομένης … τῆς φύσεως) tucked inside the accusative-and-infinitive. On the belief itself, see fable 340.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ὕαινα θεασαμένη ἀλώπεκα ἐμέμφετο αὐτὴν ὅτι φίλην θέλουσαν αὐτῇ γενέσθαι οὐ προσίεται.
sentences.tr: Kai dē hyaina theasamenē alōpeka emempheto autēn hoti philēn thelousan autēi genesthai ou prosietai.
sentences.l: And indeed a hyena, having caught sight of a fox, was blaming her, because she does not admit her when she wishes to become a friend to her.
sentences.i: And so a hyena caught sight of a fox and reproached her for not accepting her, when she wished to be her friend.
sentences.n: The pronouns all point one way: the hyena is doing the blaming and the wishing, the fox is the one who will not receive her. οὐ προσίεται stays in the present after the past ἐμέμφετο — Greek keeps the tense the words had when they were thought, where English shifts it back.

sentences.t: Κἀκείνη ὑποτυχοῦσα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μὴ μέμφου, τὴν δὲ σὴν φύσιν, δι’ ἣν ἀγνοῶ πότερον ὡς φίλῃ ἢ ὡς φίλῳ σοι χρήσομαι. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinē hypotychousa eipen· « All’ eme mē memphou, tēn de sēn physin, di’ hēn agnoō poteron hōs philēi ē hōs philōi soi chrēsomai. »
sentences.l: And she, taking-up-the-word, said: « Well, do not blame me, but your own nature, on account of which I do not know whether I shall deal with you as with a female friend or as with a male friend. »
sentences.i: And she took up the word and said: « Do not blame me, but your own nature — because of it I cannot tell whether I am to treat you as a woman friend or as a man. »
sentences.n: Κἀκείνη is καὶ ἐκείνη run together by crasis. The whole retort hangs on two endings of one word: φίλῃ feminine, φίλῳ masculine, where English must find two phrases. χράομαι takes the dative of the person dealt with.

A moral that is only a heading: πρός with the accusative and no verb at all, where the collection elsewhere fills the frame out with ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος, 'the story is well-timed'. ἀμφίβολος is what can be taken two ways at once, as at fable 182. The line is printed without a closing full stop.
